title: This Bengaluru startup is training dogs and AI to sniff out cancer early
excerpt: Dognosis, a Bengaluru startup, pairs trained sniffer dogs with AI to flag early cancer from a breath sample. It is a prescreening tool in trials, not a proven diagnostic.
content_html:
Dognosis pairs trained sniffer dogs with artificial intelligence to flag cancer from a breath sample. It is a charming idea aimed at a real problem, with equally real caveats: this is prescreening in trials, not a proven diagnostic.

A dog’s nose has long outclassed most laboratory kit, and a two-year-old Bengaluru startup called Dognosis is betting it can turn that biological talent into a screening tool.

The company pairs trained sniffer dogs with sensors and artificial intelligence to flag early signs of cancer from a single breath sample, the latest entry in a busy field where AI is being pointed at cancer detection.

The process is disarmingly simple at the patient’s end. You breathe into a mask, which is then couriered to Dognosis’s facility, a farm outside Bengaluru, where beagles, labradors and Dutch shepherds sniff the sample.

As they do, sensors and AI read the animals’ movements, respiration, brain activity and body language, translating a pause or a wag into structured data. The premise is that tumours leave a chemical signature in exhaled breath, one a dog can smell long before conventional tools can see it.

There is no imaging, unlike the systems trained to spot breast cancer on an X-ray, no blood draw and no biopsy. The AI layer is meant to do the unglamorous work of standardising an animal’s reaction into something repeatable.

Founded by Akash Kulgod, Dognosis says its approach targets more than 20 cancer types across seven groups, including breast, oral cavity, lung and cervical.

In Phase 2 trials published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, the company reports roughly 90% sensitivity for early-stage cancers.

Dogs trained on 10 cancer types, it adds, went on to identify an 11th they had never been shown. Those accuracy and detection figures are, for now, reported by the company and its researchers rather than independently confirmed.

The pitch makes most sense against India’s grim cancer arithmetic. The country logged about 1.5 million new cases and more than 900,000 deaths in 2024, one of the world’s heaviest caseloads, yet screening rates are strikingly low.

Roughly 1.9% of women are screened for cervical cancer, and fewer than 1% for breast or oral cancers. Much of that gap is a matter of cost, distance and the discomfort of invasive tests.

A cheap, non-invasive tool aimed at preventative healthcare could reach people the formal system never touches, which is precisely the market Dognosis is chasing.

Dognosis raised a $1.5m pre-seed in 2024 and has since closed a further, undisclosed round, with Accel India and Caffeinated Capital among its backers. Neither has put a figure on the latest round.

The roadmap is ambitious. Kulgod plans an at-home, multi-cancer prescreening test in India next year, priced at a few thousand rupees.

A Phase 3 trial began in April across 10 hospitals, aiming to enrol about 10,000 participants, and the company is targeting a million tests a year with a one-week turnaround, run by around 30 dogs. A US facility is pencilled in for late 2027 or early 2028.

There is a regulatory wrinkle worth flagging. Kulgod notes that Dognosis needs no Indian regulatory approval, because a prescreening tool is not classed as a diagnostic device.

That lowers the barrier to launch, but it also means the technology could reach patients without clearing the bar a formal diagnostic would have to.

A positive result is a prompt to see a doctor, not a verdict, and the distinction is one the company will need to communicate carefully.

The caveats matter. This is a prescreening tool designed to flag who should seek further tests, not a replacement for diagnosis, and the trials remain early.

There is also a certain irony in the endgame, since Dognosis eventually wants to replace the dogs with sensors, distilling the nose into hardware.

Whether or not that works, the underlying idea is a serious one: using the dog’s nose as a biosensor standardised by AI, and aiming it squarely at a screening gap conventional medicine has struggled to close.

content_html_zh:
Dognosis 将训练有素的嗅探犬与人工智能配对，从呼吸样本中标记癌症。 这是一个针对实际问题的迷人想法，但也有同样实际的警告：这是试验中的预筛选，而不是经过验证的诊断。

狗的鼻子早已超越了大多数实验室工具，班加罗尔一家成立两年的初创公司 Dognosis 押注它可以将这种生物天赋转化为筛查工具。

该公司将训练有素的嗅探犬与传感器和人工智能配对，从单一呼吸样本中标记出癌症的早期迹象，这是人工智能在癌症检测这一繁忙领域的最新进展。

对于患者来说，这个过程非常简单。 你对着口罩呼吸，然后口罩被运送到多诺西斯的工厂，这是班加罗尔郊外的一个农场，比格犬、拉布拉多犬和荷兰牧羊犬在那里嗅样本。

当它们这样做时，传感器和人工智能会读取动物的动作、呼吸、大脑活动和肢体语言，将停顿或摇摆转化为结构化数据。 前提是肿瘤在呼出的气体中留下化学特征，狗早在传统工具看到它之前就能闻到这种化学特征。

与通过 X 射线发现乳腺癌的系统不同，它不需要成像，不需要抽血，也不需要活检。 人工智能层的目的是将动物的反应标准化为可重复的东西，这是一项乏味的工作。

Dognosis 由 Akash Kulgod 创立，表示其方法针对 7 个组别 20 多种癌症类型，包括乳腺癌、口腔癌、肺癌和宫颈癌。

在《临床肿瘤学杂志》上发表的 2 期试验中，该公司报告对早期癌症的敏感性约为 90%。

报告补充说，狗接受了 10 种癌症类型的训练，随后识别出了它们从未见过的 11 种癌症。 目前，这些准确性和检测数据由该公司及其研究人员报告，而不是独立确认。

面对印度严峻的癌症形势，这一宣传最有意义。 2024 年，该国新增病例约 150 万例，死亡人数超过 90 万，是世界上病例数最多的国家之一，但筛查率却低得惊人。

大约 1.9% 的女性接受了宫颈癌筛查，不到 1% 的女性接受了乳腺癌或口腔癌筛查。 这种差距很大程度上是由于成本、距离和侵入性测试的不适感造成的。

一种旨在预防性医疗保健的廉价、非侵入性工具可以覆盖正规系统从未触及的人们，这正是 Dognosis 正在追逐的市场。

Dognosis 于 2024 年筹集了 150 万美元的种子前资金，此后又完成了另一轮未公开的融资，其支持者包括 Accel India 和 Caffelined Capital。 双方都没有公布最新一轮的具体数字。

该路线图雄心勃勃。 Kulgod 计划明年在印度进行家庭多种癌症预筛查测试，价格为数千卢比。

第三阶段试验于 4 月份在 10 家医院开始，旨在招募约 10,000 名参与者，该公司的目标是每年进行 100 万次测试，周转时间为一周，由约 30 只狗进行。 美国工厂预计将于 2027 年底或 2028 年初建成。

有一个监管问题值得警惕。 Kulgod 指出，Dognosis 不需要印度监管机构的批准，因为预筛选工具不属于诊断设备。

这降低了推出的门槛，但这也意味着该技术可以在不清除正式诊断门槛的情况下接触到患者。

阳性结果是提示去看医生，而不是判决，公司需要仔细沟通这一区别。

注意事项很重要。 这是一种预筛选工具，旨在标记谁应该寻求进一步的测试，而不是替代诊断，而且试验仍处于早期阶段。

最后的游戏也有一定的讽刺意味，因为 Dognosis 最终想要用传感器取代狗，将鼻子提炼成硬件。

无论这是否有效，其基本想法都是严肃的：使用狗的鼻子作为人工智能标准化的生物传感器，并将其直接瞄准传统医学难以弥补的筛查空白。
